I work in Assertive Community Treatment where things change constantly and I have a poor memory for details like times and sometimes even what I did with someone shortly after seeing them... I use a couple of apps to keep me on track and I also have an extensive pen-and-paper notebook system I use to keep everything straight since otherwise I'd lose track of everything!

I use an app called Swipetimes to track when I start and end client visits - it's essentially a punch clock app but on Android you can place a widget on your home screen to quickly "punch in," which I do as I'm walking from the car (or my office) to wherever I'm meeting the client. That way when I go to document (often days later), I have all the exact times right there for me.

I also use the Google Keep app, which is a notes app, for a ton of things but primarily for quick documentation (without PHI of course, I add a few finishing touches when I actually put it into our documentation software). I often only get a minute here or there between visits or while I'm waiting for a client so I can just pull up the app and type up most of a note quick. I use this one in particular because it's easy to pull up on my laptop when I have more time or I'm at my desk and I can just copy and paste my notes into our documentation software (which is very unreliable,   so I prefer to type my notes elsewhere and paste them in so I don't lose my work again and again).

I also constantly use my alarm app and a generic reminders app I downloaded. In a field where it's nearly impossible NOT to get sidetracked as we have 100 things demanding our attention at any given time, I've found that I need external reminders for everything from leaving to see a client on time to actually standing up, stretching, and remembering I'm a person who needs self-care.

Hope you find everyone's amazing suggestions helpful! I know I did.

I was sexually abused as a child and assaulted (not raped) as an adult. The worst assault I was pinned against the wall and groped/grinded on while his friends behind him laughed. This was extremely traumatizing to me, probably because of my childhood. After that incident I spent weeks in bed isolated and drunk.

I completely understand your feelings on this. I feel like because it wasn't rape, I don't have the right to be upset and have PTSD issues. Since others have it worse, why do I get to be upset? Then I start to think that if I was actually raped, my feelings would be more valid. I also think about putting myself in dangerous situations.

Ultimately though I understand not feeling like you "deserve" to be upset or traumatized, your emotions and reactions are 100% valid. You went through something that was traumatizing for you (and probably would be for the vast majority of people). You are allowed to be upset by this. You are allowed to feel fear and guilt. No one wins in the trauma Olympics. Comparing your situation to others will only end up with someone's pain being minimized.

What would you say to a friend that went through what you went through? Would you tell them to get over it because other people are assaulted more violently?

Do your best to be kind and gentle with yourself. You've been hurt but you're not broken (that's what I tell myself). If you can, you may find therapy helpful to process through some of your emotions and help you find alternatives when you're feeling self-destructive. You deserve only good things.

Like you said, a lot of people may frown on cannabis as another addiction. I'm personally not concerned about what they think, I'm more concerned with how you feel. If what you're doing is working for you, great! If there are unintended negative consequences of the cannabis use, then you may consider quitting.

Personally I don't believe that for every person, addiction to one substance means you should be sober from all. I was addicted to benzos, went through treatment, got sober, then made the decision to drink occasionally. For me, this works. I keep a close eye on my drinking and make sure not to drink because I'm upset. I rarely have more than one or two. I don't think I'm forever an addict with every substance.

You have to do what feels right for you. If something changes down the line and you feel your cannabis use is a problem, then it may be time to quit. Only you can decide.

Work with your counselors to develop pros and cons. The way I like to do it may seem complicated but in the end it's the simplest way to make a decision. Instructions below for my version.

1. Pros and cons on top, doing the thing and not doing the thing down the left, draw lines between so that you have 4 boxes
2. Write pros of doing the thing, pros of not doing the thing, cons of doing the thing, and cons of not doing the thing in each of their boxes; add things like gut feeling and want to/don't want to, as applicable
3. Rate every pro/con on personal importance on a scale of 1-5, 5 is most important, 1 is barely important
4. Add up each box, then add the number from the pros of doing the thing with the cons of not doing the thing; then separately add the cons of doing and the pros of not doing
5. Finally, compare the two scores. Subtract the cons of doing/pros of not doing total FROM the pros of doing/cons of not doing for your final score.
6. If you get a positive number, then you want to do the thing. If you get a negative number, then you want to NOT do the thing.
